In this profile it stands out as clinically implausible relative to the other items, whereas the other maladaptive strategies center on vigilance, escape, and social evaluation.

vignette:
Amir is a 22-year-old auditor who, until six months ago, had felt his life was progressing exactly as planned. That changed the night his then-boyfriend raped him in their shared apartment. The assault itself was a terrifying violation, but it was the things his partner said afterwards—the casual dismissal, the cruel justifications that twisted the blame back onto Amir—that planted the seeds of a profound and lasting humiliation. The scent of the sandalwood cologne his ex always wore seemed to permeate the room, an olfactory anchor to the worst moments of his life. For weeks, Amir functioned on autopilot, but as the initial shock receded, a new and terrifying reality began to take shape, governed by the echoes of that night.

The triggers were unpredictable at first, ambushing him in the middle of his workday. A senior partner at his firm wore a similar sandalwood cologne, and the first time he caught the scent in a meeting, the conference room seemed to tilt on its axis. The smell didn't just bring back a memory; it brought a hot, visceral wave of shame that confirmed his deepest fear: that he was weak and fundamentally flawed. He found himself thinking, "Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation." This pattern repeated itself. When a manager, trying to be encouraging, used a phrase his ex had often used—"Don't be so dramatic"—Amir felt his face flush, certain that his own damage was suddenly visible to everyone at the table. These moments cemented his belief that he was permanently humiliated by what had happened.

His body began to operate under a new set of rules, treating the world as a hostile territory. Amir felt constantly tense, his muscles coiled tight as if bracing for an impact. This pervasive sense of being on high alert made any unfamiliar environment feel impossibly threatening. When assigned to a new client, he would spend the first hour not reviewing their books, but mapping the building’s layout, his mind fixated on escape routes. He learned to position himself in the chair closest to the door in every meeting, a strategy that offered a sliver of control in situations that felt overwhelmingly dangerous. He found he couldn't go to new restaurants or stores because he couldn't assess the danger. Sudden movements from colleagues—someone standing up too quickly or reaching across a desk—would cause him to flinch, his body reacting to a threat only he could perceive.

This deep conviction that he was permanently broken and shameful began to dictate his every move. He was certain that if people looked at him too closely, they would see the weakness he felt branded on him. This fear drove him to wear baggy, concealing sweaters and jackets, even in the warm office, hoping to render himself invisible. More consequentially, he started to systematically avoid any situation that involved evaluation. He, an auditor whose job was to evaluate, became terrified of being judged himself. He began finding excuses to miss client presentations and dodged his own performance reviews, volunteering for tedious back-office work to stay out of the spotlight. Yet, each act of avoidance only reinforced his negative beliefs. The brief relief of escaping a meeting would quickly curdle into a crushing wave of self-loathing. "I used to be a happy person," he would think, sitting alone at his desk long after everyone else had gone home, "but now I am always miserable, hiding like a coward."

His strategies and his hypervigilance became a self-sustaining loop. The constant, tense scanning of his environment made him more likely to notice things that would otherwise be innocuous, like seeing people misbehaving on the street, which he now interpreted through the lens of moral violation, a reminder of his ex’s callousness. On one occasion, the scent from a stranger on the subway was so triggering that he immediately got off and spent ten minutes by an exit, calming his racing heart. The very act of constantly planning his escape kept his body in a state of high alert. By positioning himself near doorways at work, he was also more likely to overhear snippets of conversation from the hallway, sometimes catching a phrase that would send a jolt of fear through him.

Amir finally sought therapy after receiving a formal warning from his supervisor. His avoidance of client-facing responsibilities had become a serious professional liability. He is now caught in an impossible bind: the terror of engaging with a world he perceives as dangerous, and the certainty of losing his career if he continues to hide from it. He described feeling permanently stained by the assault, but in his final words of the intake session, he confessed a desperate hope to one day feel "normal" again, to find the confident young man he was before his world shrank to the size of his fear.
